title: The Santiparva (Yudhishthira Comforted)
body:
The Santiparva (Yudhishthira Comforted)

Yudhishthira's pain of mind increased every day. Every grand hall in Hastinapur seemed to echo with the silent screams of the fallen. To him, the royal insignia and the soft cushions of the throne were but mockeries of a hollow victory. Stricken with intense remorse, he announced his final decision to his family: 'I see no joy or good in taking up the office of king or in worldly enjoyment. Sins of massive proportions have been committed for the sake of this transient wealth. I shall renounce this world, go to the deep forest, wrap my body in bark, and perform severe penances to expiate my sins. Do rule this land yourselves, leaving me free to depart.'
One by one, his brothers and Queen Draupadi rose to contest his decision, using the traditional frameworks of Kshatriya duty (Swadharma) to challenge his desire for ascetic isolation. Arjuna talked extensively of the nobility of family life and the immense good a righteous king can perform without taking Sanyasa. Bhimasena, characteristically direct and forceful, spoke with sharp, intellectual rigor: 'You talk, alas, like a dull-witted person who has committed to memory the texts of the sastras without understanding their true sense. Sanyasa is not the dharma of Kshatriyas. The duty of a Kshatriya is to live an active life and perform his proper task of protection, not to flee to the forest renouncing action.'
Nakula and Sahadeva also joined the debate, arguing that the path of active work (Karma Yoga) is the true foundation of human evolution, while Sanyasa is often beset with hidden psychological traps. Sahadeva fell at his feet, pleading, 'You are my father, my mother, my teacher, as well as my brother. Do not leave us; bear with us.'
Draupadi, her voice combining maternal grief and imperial dignity, added her voice: 'Among the duties of a king is included the inflicting of just punishment. It cannot be avoided; it is an essential part of the ruler's duty. You have meted out just punishment to evil-doers. There is no cause whatsoever for contrition. It is now your sacred duty to take up the burden of governing this land according to dharma. Cease grieving.'
Finally, Sage Vyasa spoke at length, explaining that a king's highest penance is the selfless, unattached execution of his royal duties. He persuaded Yudhishthira that to run away from the ruined kingdom was a form of cowardice, a betrayal of the Jeevas who relied upon him for protection. Yielding to this collective wisdom, Yudhishthira agreed to be crowned at Hastinapura.
But before taking up the active reins of the state, Yudhishthira sought the ultimate source of spiritual and political wisdom. Led by Sree Krishna and Sage Vyasa, the Pandavas journeyed to the battlefield of Kurukshetra, where the great grandsire Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows (Sharashayya), waiting for the auspicious northward movement of the sun (Uttarayan) to leave his physical frame. This final meeting between the dying patriarch and the newly crowned king forms the monumental Santiparva—the section of peace and cosmic instruction.
